briefing:
SITUATION BRIEFING — Round 10 (FINAL)

Day 10 of the Suwałki Crisis. The military phase is over. The political transformation of Europe has begun.

MILITARY: Russian withdrawal from Lithuania COMPLETE as of Day 9, 11:42 CET. NATO has full control of the Suwałki Corridor. Suwałki Shield Force activation beginning — US, Polish, Lithuanian, and German elements forming permanent brigade garrison. All NATO forces beginning phased de-escalation. Russian forces back in Kaliningrad (depleted) and Belarus (transiting to Russia).

BELARUS: Lukashenko has FLED. Military provisional council under Col. Kastsyukevich declared transitional government. Free elections promised in 90 days. Political prisoners being released. Russian military transit through Belarus CLOSED. This is the single most consequential political shift — if Belarus democratizes, Russia loses its western strategic buffer entirely.

DIPLOMATIC: Geneva Process formal talks open Day 10. Russia (Lavrov/Gerasimov-directed) shows unprecedented willingness to discuss arms control. Key agenda: European security architecture, NATO-Russia communications, conventional arms control, nuclear risk reduction, accountability mechanisms. China has observer status.

ECONOMIC: Recovery underway. Oil at $98, euro at 1.02. Baltic shipping fully restored. Russian economy in deep recession — GDP projected to contract 8% this year. Lithuania reconstruction beginning with €50B European fund.

CASUALTIES (FINAL): NATO: ~15 KIA (4 PL airmen at Łask, 3 DE EFP soldiers, 1 US V Corps soldier, ~7 PL/LT combat deaths), ~45 WIA. Russia: ~350 KIA, ~800 WIA, ~450 POWs (returned). Civilian: ~25 killed, 23,000+ displaced.
narrative:
At 11:42 CET on Day 9, the last Russian soldier crossed from Lithuanian territory into Belarus — a young conscript from Pskov who looked bewildered as OSCE monitors recorded the moment. Lithuania's Prime Minister, standing at the border crossing, declared: 'Lithuanian sovereignty is restored. Not one centimeter of our land remains under foreign occupation.' NATO Secretary General Rutte confirmed full withdrawal verification at 14:00, and the world let out a collective breath it had been holding for nine days.

But the Suwałki Crisis's final act played out not in Lithuania but in Belarus. At 08:00, as Russian forces were completing their transit, the Belarusian military effectively split. The 38th Air Assault Brigade and elements of the 103rd Airborne Brigade declared themselves 'in defense of the Belarusian constitution' and refused to recognize orders from Lukashenko's KGB-dominated security apparatus. Lukashenko, reportedly in a panic, ordered Russian forces transiting Belarus to 'restore order' — but General Gerasimov, already furious about the entire Suwałki debacle, refused, telling Minsk that 'Russia will not shed blood to prop up your regime while our boys are coming home in body bags.' By 16:00, Lukashenko had fled Minsk by helicopter to an undisclosed location — reportedly a dacha outside Moscow.

The Belarusian military's provisional council, led by the 38th Brigade's Colonel Syarhei Kastsyukevich, declared a 'transitional military administration' and immediately announced three things: free elections within 90 days, the release of all political prisoners, and the closure of Belarusian territory to Russian military transit. The streets of Minsk erupted in scenes reminiscent of 2020 — but this time, the military was on the people's side. The EU immediately signaled willingness to engage with the transitional government, while Russia — humiliated and exhausted — could only issue a pro forma statement about 'internal Belarusian affairs.'

The Geneva Process preliminary talks confirmed Day 10 as the opening of formal negotiations. Russia's delegation, now led by Lavrov but reportedly under instruction from Gerasimov rather than Putin, signaled willingness to discuss substantive arms control and confidence-building measures — a dramatic shift from the pre-crisis posture of rejecting all Western security frameworks.

headlines: MINSK IS FREE: Belarus declares democracy after Lukashenko flees
THE COST: 390 dead, 23,000 displaced, $500B, and the closest nuclear call since Cuba
NEW EUROPE: Suwałki Crisis reshapes continental security for a generation
GENEVA HOPE: Post-crisis talks could produce first US-Russia arms accord in decades
GERASIMOV: The Russian general who stopped the nuclear clock
surprises: In the chaos of Lukashenko's flight, Belarusian opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya — who had been in exile in Vilnius since 2020 — crossed the Lithuanian-Belarusian border at Medininkai (the same crossing where Kowalski was freed). She was greeted by Col. Kastsyukevich and a crowd of thousands. Her words: 'I left through this border in tears. I return through it in hope.'

Japanese PM Shigeru Ishiba, shaken by the China Taiwan Strait exercises during the crisis, announces Japan will increase defense spending to 3% of GDP — the most dramatic Japanese security policy shift since 1945. The Suwałki Crisis's ripple effects are reshaping security architecture not just in Europe but globally.
